claims.claim: An energy source is renewable if it is naturally replenished on a human timescale — flow-limited in any given moment but effectively inexhaustible over time — in contrast to finite fossil fuels and nuclear fuel.
The main renewable sources are solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, and biomass (biomass includes wood and wood waste, municipal solid waste, landfill gas, biogas, and biofuels).

In 2025, renewables supplied about 9% of total U.S. primary energy consumption (about 8.8 quadrillion BTU) but about 24% of U.S. utility-scale electricity generation — the electricity share is much larger than the total-energy share.

Within U.S. electricity in 2025, wind supplied about 11% of total generation, solar about 7%, hydropower about 6%, biomass about 1%, and geothermal less than 1%; the renewable share of utility-scale generation rose from about 12% in 1990 to about 24% in 2025.

Globally, renewables generated about one-third (33%) of electricity in 2024, led by hydropower (~14%), wind (~8%), and solar PV (~7%); renewables plus nuclear together covered about two-fifths (40%) of world electricity generation for the first time.

Capacity (installed generating capability, measured in MW or GW) is distinct from generation (energy actually produced, measured in MWh or TWh); the capacity factor is the ratio of energy a unit actually produced to the energy it could have produced running continuously at full power over the same period.

In 2024, U.S. annual capacity factors were about 91% for nuclear, 65% for geothermal, 35% for conventional hydropower, 34% for wind, and 23% for solar photovoltaics — so an installed-capacity share overstates wind and solar relative to their generation share.

Wind and solar are variable (intermittent): their output follows the weather and time of day rather than demand, so integrating them relies on energy storage, flexible dispatchable plants, transmission, and demand management. U.S. utility-scale battery storage nearly doubled in 2024, with about 14.3 GW added to roughly 15.5 GW already installed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The reported U.S. renewable electricity share depends on the reporting year and on whether small-scale (rooftop) solar is included.
positions: EIA's renewable-sources overview (April 2024 preliminary data) states renewables were about 21% of U.S. electricity generation in 2023.
EIA's electricity-in-the-US page states renewables were about 24% of U.S. utility-scale generation in 2025.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the most recent EIA figure (about 24% of utility-scale generation in 2025) for the headline electricity share, dates it explicitly, and notes that these figures are for utility-scale generation and exclude distributed rooftop solar; it presents the ~9% primary-energy share for the same year to make the electricity-vs-primary-energy contrast.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Capacity factors vary year to year and by vintage of the fleet.
positions: 2024 final values (EIA EPM Table 6.07.B): nuclear 90.8%, geothermal 64.6%, hydro 34.6%, wind 34.3%, solar PV 23.2%.
Other years differ slightly (e.g., nuclear has run 92-93% in several recent years).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson rounds the 2024 final values and dates them to 2024, and frames capacity factor as a structural difference between variable and dispatchable sources rather than a fixed constant.

rightsIssues: U.S. EIA sources are U.S. government works, public domain; used as REFERENCE_ONLY factual data with original wording. sourceRecords.title: Renewable energy explained
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the definition of renewable energy ('energy from sources that are naturally replenishing but flow-limited... virtually inexhaustible') and the five main sources (biomass, hydropower, geothermal, wind, solar). Also states renewables were ~9% of total U.S. energy consumption (8.2 quads) and ~21% of U.S. electricity generation in 2023 (April 2024 preliminary data); the lesson uses the newer 2025 utility-scale figure for the headline electricity share. U.S. government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Sources of energy — what is energy explained
sourceRecords.notes: Reused existing registry source id. Supports the renewable-versus-nonrenewable framing: renewable sources are replenished in a short time, nonrenewable sources (fossil fuels, nuclear fuel) exist in fixed amounts. U.S. government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Electricity in the United States — electricity explained
sourceRecords.notes: Page text parsed via curl. Supports the 2025 U.S. utility-scale electricity shares: natural gas ~41%, nuclear ~18%, coal ~17%, renewables ~24% total (wind ~11%, solar ~7%, hydro ~6%, biomass ~1%, geothermal <1%); total utility-scale generation ~4.43 trillion kWh in 2025; renewables were ~12% of utility-scale generation in 1990. U.S. government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Solar and battery storage to make up 81% of new U.S. electric-generating capacity in 2024 (Today in Energy)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the grid-integration claim: solar and battery storage were expected to be 81% of new U.S. capacity in 2024 (solar 36.4 GW, storage 14.3 GW), with U.S. battery-storage capacity nearly doubling as ~14.3 GW was added to ~15.5 GW already installed. Used to illustrate storage as a response to variability. U.S. government work, public domain.
